questions.q: What is a customer master record, as defined in this lesson?
options: The authoritative, relatively stable record of every party an organization sells to, bills, or supports
A single table of every transaction a customer has ever made
A marketing-only list of email addresses used for newsletters
The list of employees who are permitted to contact customers
questions.explain: A customer master record holds stable identifying and classification attributes — ID, names, addresses, tax IDs, status — not transactional data that changes with every order.

questions.q: What is the 'party model' used by most MDM platforms?
options: A generic 'party' entity that can be a person or an organization, with a role like customer or vendor layered on top
A rule that only political organizations can be stored as customers
A model that stores only corporate customers, never individuals
A naming convention for database tables, unrelated to customer data
questions.explain: The party model separates the entity itself (person or organization) from the role it plays, which lets one party hold multiple roles, such as being both a customer and a vendor.

questions.q: Why does one real-world customer often end up as several different records across systems, per this lesson's example?
options: Each system captured the customer independently, with inconsistent names and no shared identifier
Customers are legally required to register separately with every department
It only happens when a customer deliberately provides false information
Database software automatically duplicates every new customer record
questions.explain: CRM, billing, and e-commerce each recorded 'Acme Inc.' under a slightly different name with its own system-generated ID, because no shared key tied the records together.

questions.q: In a corporate customer hierarchy, what does the 'ultimate parent' represent?
options: The top entity in the hierarchy that related subsidiary accounts roll up to
The single employee responsible for approving all customer discounts
The customer's original founding date
The smallest subsidiary at the bottom of the corporate structure
questions.explain: Subsidiaries place their own orders and get their own invoices, but roll up to the ultimate parent for enterprise-wide views like credit limits and discount tiers.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why is getting a corporate customer hierarchy right often harder than deduplicating the base customer records?
options: Because the correct hierarchy is a business judgment about who controls purchasing decisions, not just a data-matching exercise
Because hierarchies never need to be updated once created
Because corporate hierarchies are always identical to the company's public org chart
Because deduplication is actually impossible for B2B customers
questions.explain: Deduplication finds records that refer to the same party; the hierarchy then requires a judgment call about corporate structure and control, which changes with mergers and restructuring.
